# Introduction 


# Beliefs and Belief Systems 


# Climate Change in Congress 


# Data and Analysis 

To examine the feasibility of measuring belief systems and information sources among members of Congress, I use floor speeches from the *Congressional Record* given during three debates over climate and energy legislation. The first is the debate over cap-and-trade in the 111th Congress, the second is the debate over the Inflation Reduction Act (IRA) in the 117th Congress, and the third is the debate over the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBB) in the 119th Congress. Below, I describe how the speeches were collected, how they were coded, and the measures used in the analysis.

## Congressional Speeches

Congressional speeches were obtained from the daily edition of the *Congressional Record* using the GovInfo service of the Government Publishing Office, which allows a full-text search of each item printed in the Record. I built two collections of speeches. The first covers 2000 to 2012 and includes any item from the House, the Senate, or the Extensions of Remarks that contains the phrases "climate change," "global warming," "greenhouse gas," "cap and trade," "national energy tax," "cap and tax," or "carbon tax," or that names one of the major climate bills of the period, such as the American Clean Energy and Security Act (Waxman-Markey). The second covers 2018 to 2026 and uses the same phrases along with the names of the Green New Deal, Build Back Better, the IRA, and the OBBB, as well as phrases that refer to clean energy tax credits in 2025. The Daily Digest, which is the Record's own summary of each day, was dropped. The searches returned 6,386 items for the first period and 5,388 items for the second.

Each item was then split into speeches. A speech is one member's turn on the floor, which begins at the line that names the speaker and ends when the next speaker or the presiding officer is recognized. Turns by the presiding officer were dropped, and material that a member asked to have printed in the Record (e.g., bill text, letters, and articles) was removed where it could be identified. Speeches that are published twice in the Record were kept once.

Many of these speeches mention climate change only in passing. As a result, I kept a speech only if it had at least 50 words and met one of three rules. The first rule keeps a speech that has three or more mentions of the climate phrases used in the search and at least two mentions per 1,000 words. The second rule keeps a speech that has two or more mentions when the title of the item in the Record names the topic. The third rule keeps a speech that names one of the climate bills of its period and has three or more mentions of a broader set of energy terms (e.g., clean energy, fossil fuels, and emissions), with at least two mentions per 1,000 words. The third rule is needed because much of the debate over the IRA and the OBBB involved energy tax credits and energy production, and many of those speeches do not use the climate phrases. This resulted in `r fmt(n_ct)` speeches from 2000 to 2012 and `r fmt(n_ira)` speeches from 2018 to 2026, for a total of `r fmt(n_speeches)` speeches. The party and state of each speaker come from the GovInfo record for the item, and each speaker was matched to their DW-NOMINATE scores from Voteview.

From these speeches, I coded those given by Democrats and Republicans during the three debates. I define each debate by a window that begins when the legislative vehicle for the bill first moved and ends with the final disposition of the bill. The cap-and-trade window begins with the release of the Waxman-Markey discussion draft on March 31, 2009 and ends on July 22, 2010, when Senate leaders set aside the climate bill. The IRA window begins when the Senate adopted the budget resolution for fiscal year 2022 on August 11, 2021 and ends when the bill was signed on August 16, 2022. The OBBB window begins when the House adopted the budget resolution for fiscal year 2025 on February 25, 2025 and ends when the bill was signed on July 4, 2025. As shown in @tbl-sample, this resulted in `r fmt(n_coded)` speeches given by `r n_coded_members` members.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-sample
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "Coded speeches by debate"
knitr::kable(tab_sample[, setdiff(names(tab_sample), "Period")],
             format = "pipe", format.args = list(big.mark = ","))
```

## Coding Beliefs and Information Sources

Speeches were coded using a codebook that I developed for this project. Following the Advocacy Coalition Framework, the codebook organizes beliefs into the deep core, policy core, and secondary tiers of a belief system [@jenkins-smithAdvocacyCoalitionFramework2018]. The codebook contains `r n_concepts` concepts, and each concept is written as a proposition with which a speaker can agree or disagree. As shown in @tbl-concepts, there are `r n_tier[["Deep core"]]` deep core concepts that involve general values such as the role of government and fairness, `r n_tier[["Policy core"]]` policy core concepts that involve the climate problem and the costs and benefits of addressing it, and `r n_tier[["Secondary"]]` secondary concepts that involve specific policy instruments. The concepts were chosen to reflect how members of Congress argue about climate and energy on the floor, and they were revised over several rounds of pilot coding with a stratified sample of 150 speeches.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-concepts
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "Belief concepts in the codebook"
#| tbl-colwidths: [15, 9, 76]
knitr::kable(tab_concepts, format = "pipe")
```

The unit of coding is the statement, which is a passage where the speaker expresses a position on one concept [@leifeldDiscourseNetworkAnalysis2017]. For each statement, the coder records the concept, whether the speaker agrees or disagrees with the proposition, and the intensity of the stance on a four-point scale that ranges from strong disagreement to strong agreement. Beliefs can be understood as probability distributions that have both a central tendency and a degree of uncertainty [@nowlinPolicyBeliefsBelief2024]. To capture uncertainty, the coder also records whether the speaker hedges the stance by qualifying it or presenting it as tentative (e.g., "may," "might," or "I think"). Each combination of concept and stance is coded at most once per speech, and each code must be supported by a verbatim quote from the speech of no more than 40 words. Only the positions of the speaker are coded, and a position is not inferred from the party of the speaker or from silence on a concept.

Information sources are coded separately from beliefs. A source is anything outside of the speaker's own reasoning that is offered as evidence, expertise, or testimony, such as a scientific body, an agency analysis, a news report, or a constituent. For each source, the coder records the type of source using 17 categories (e.g., science, government analysis, business, advocacy groups, the media, and constituents), whether the source is named or generic, the form of the evidence taken from the source, and whether the speaker relies on the source or disputes it. Scientific sources are also coded for whether they are cited for a claim that is in line with the scientific consensus on climate change or a claim that disputes it. Additionally, each source is linked to the concepts that it is used to support, which connects the information that members cite to the beliefs that they express. Finally, for each speech the coder records the bill that is being debated, the stance of the speaker on that bill, and whether climate or energy is the main subject of the speech.

## Coding Procedure

The speeches were coded by a large language model (LLM), Claude Opus 5.5 from Anthropic, which follows recent work that uses LLMs as coders that are guided by a codebook [@haltermanCodebookLLMsEvaluating2025]. The instructions given to the model were the coding rules of the codebook reproduced word for word, along with the format for the output. The speeches were placed in a random order and divided into batches of 10 speeches. Each batch was coded by a separate instance of the model that had access to only the instructions and the speeches in its batch. As a result, no instance of the model saw the codes produced by another, and each batch contained a mix of debates, parties, and chambers. The text given to the model included the name, party, and state of the speaker, and the instructions direct the coder to not infer a position from party.

After coding, each batch was checked by a script. The script confirmed that every speech was coded once, that all codes used the values allowed by the codebook, and that every quote appears verbatim in the text of the speech. All `r fmt(n_statements + n_sources)` quotes passed this check. Across the `r fmt(n_coded)` speeches, the model coded `r fmt(n_statements)` statements and `r fmt(n_sources)` information sources, and `r n_no_statement` speeches contained no codable statement (e.g., tributes and procedural remarks). The settings that govern randomness in the model could not be fixed, so the codes are not exactly reproducible. For this reason, the raw output of each batch was archived.

Codes produced by an LLM need to be validated against the judgment of human coders. In the pilot, two independent rounds of coding of the same 150 speeches by the model agreed on which concepts were present in a speech, with a median $\kappa$ of 0.88 across the concepts. However, agreement between two runs of the same model is likely to overstate agreement with human coders. To assess validity, a stratified subset of `r n_human_coding` speeches will be coded independently by two trained human coders using the same codebook, and agreement between the human codes and the model codes will be assessed using Krippendorff's $\alpha$ [@krippendorffContentAnalysisIntroduction2003]. **[Results of the human coding and the agreement statistics to be added.]**

## Analysis

The analysis is descriptive. To examine whether beliefs can be measured as probability distributions, I examine both the position and the uncertainty of each belief. For position, I use the direction and the intensity of the statements on each concept. For uncertainty, I use the share of statements on each concept that are hedged as well as the dispersion of stances across the speeches that address the concept, since beliefs that are held with less certainty are likely to be expressed less consistently. To examine the information sources cited by members, I use the share of speeches that cite each type of source. I measure sources by their presence in a speech and not by the number of sources cited, since a small number of speeches cite many sources. To compare the three debates, I define the salience of a belief or an information source as the share of speeches in a debate where it appears, and I compare salience across the debates and between Democrats and Republicans. Finally, some speeches address climate or energy only briefly, so I also examine whether the results differ when the analysis is limited to speeches where climate or energy is the main subject.

# Results

<!-- DRAFT (Claude). Results use the LLM codes as coded. Numbers are inline R and will update when these are done; the interpretive sentences should be checked again then. -->

Speeches that contained at least one codable statement included an average of `r stmt_per_speech` statements. Members also tended to state their positions forcefully, as `r pct_strong` percent of statements were coded at the strongest level of agreement or disagreement. Below, I first describe the positions and the uncertainty of the beliefs expressed in the speeches, then the information sources that members cited, and finally how the salience of beliefs differed across the three debates.

## Belief Positions

@fig-positions shows the mean position of Democrats and Republicans on each concept in each debate. Position ranges from −2 (strong disagreement) to 2 (strong agreement), and the size of each point reflects the share of the party's speeches that address the concept. As expected, the parties take opposite positions on most of the policy core and secondary concepts. In the cap-and-trade debate, `r opposite["CT", "n_both"]` concepts were addressed in at least 10 speeches by each party, and the mean positions of the two parties were on opposite sides of the scale on `r opposite["CT", "n_opposite"]` of them. In the IRA and OBBB debates, the parties were on opposite sides on `r opposite["IRA", "n_opposite"]` of `r opposite["IRA", "n_both"]` and `r opposite["OBBB", "n_opposite"]` of `r opposite["OBBB", "n_both"]` concepts, respectively.

```{r}
#| label: fig-positions
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Mean position on each concept by debate and party. Point size is proportional to the share of the party's speeches that address the concept; concepts addressed in fewer than five of a party's speeches are omitted. Horizontal lines separate the deep core, policy core, and secondary concepts."
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 8
plot_positions()
```

The clearest division is over the climate problem itself. Every Democratic speech that addressed whether climate change is happening and human caused (PC1) agreed with the proposition. Among Republicans, `r agr("PC1", "CT", "R")` percent of the speeches that addressed PC1 in the cap-and-trade debate agreed with it, as did `r agr("PC3", "CT", "R")` percent of the speeches that addressed the reliability of climate science (PC3). By the IRA debate, only `r bn("PC1", "IRA", "R")` Republican speeches addressed PC1, and none of them agreed with it. Republicans instead focused on the costs of climate and clean energy policy (PC4), which was their most salient policy core belief in all three debates. At least `r min(agr("PC4", "CT", "R"), agr("PC4", "IRA", "R"), agr("PC4", "OBBB", "R"))` percent of the Republican speeches that addressed PC4 agreed that these policies impose unacceptable costs, while `r agr("PC4", "CT", "D")` percent of the Democratic speeches that addressed it agreed in the cap-and-trade debate and none did in the later debates.

The secondary beliefs follow the bills under debate. In the cap-and-trade debate, `r sal("SC1", "CT", "R")` percent of Republican speeches addressed cap-and-trade (SC1), and `r agr("SC1", "CT", "R")` percent of those speeches supported it. Democrats were less unified, as `r agr("SC1", "CT", "D")` percent of the Democratic speeches that addressed SC1 supported it. Republicans supported expanding domestic fossil fuel production (SC7) in nearly every speech that addressed it. Democratic support for SC7 fell from `r agr("SC7", "CT", "D")` percent of the speeches that addressed it in the cap-and-trade debate to `r agr("SC7", "IRA", "D")` percent in the IRA debate and `r agr("SC7", "OBBB", "D")` percent in the OBBB debate.

The deep core beliefs show less division. Republicans agreed that government should minimize intervention in energy markets (DC1) in every speech that addressed it, while few Democrats addressed DC1 at all. However, both parties agreed with the propositions on fairness to disadvantaged communities (DC2) and on fiscal restraint (DC4). Under the codebook, a speaker who argues that a bill is paid for or reduces the deficit agrees with DC4, so the agreement of Democrats with DC4 (`r agr("DC4", "IRA", "D")` percent of the speeches that addressed it in the IRA debate) likely reflects defenses of the bill rather than opposition to it. As a result, the deep core values that members invoked were often shared, but they were applied to opposite conclusions about the bills.

## Uncertainty

Explicit hedging was rare. Only `r n_hedged` of the `r fmt(n_statements)` statements (`r pct_hedged` percent) were hedged. However, hedging was concentrated in the beliefs about the climate problem. Republicans hedged `r hedged_sci["TRUE", "R"]` percent of their statements on PC1, PC2, and PC3, compared with `r hedged_sci["TRUE", "D"]` percent for Democrats and about `r hedged_sci["FALSE", "R"]` percent for all other concepts in both parties. In the cap-and-trade debate, `r hed("PC1", "CT", "R")` percent of the Republican speeches that addressed PC1 included a hedged statement. Hedging also declined over time, from `r hedged_group["Cap-and-trade", "D"]` percent of Democratic and `r hedged_group["Cap-and-trade", "R"]` percent of Republican statements in the cap-and-trade debate to less than 1 percent in both parties in the later debates.

Since hedging was rare, the dispersion of positions within each party is likely the more informative measure of uncertainty. @tbl-dispersion shows the standard deviation of speech-level positions for each party in each debate where at least 10 of the party's speeches addressed the concept. A standard deviation near 0.5 indicates that speeches were on the same side of the proposition and differed only in intensity, while a standard deviation near or above 1 indicates that members of the same party were on both sides. In the cap-and-trade debate, Republican positions were dispersed on PC1 (`r dsp("PC1", "CT", "R")`), PC2 (`r dsp("PC2", "CT", "R")`), and the economic opportunity of clean energy (PC5, `r dsp("PC5", "CT", "R")`). The dispersion on PC1 and PC2 is consistent with the hedging on the climate problem. Democratic positions were dispersed on several secondary beliefs, including cap-and-trade (`r dsp("SC1", "CT", "D")`), EPA regulation of greenhouse gases (SC3, `r dsp("SC3", "CT", "D")`), and fossil fuel production (`r dsp("SC7", "CT", "D")`). In the IRA and OBBB debates, dispersion was lower on most concepts. Part of this decline is due to Republicans no longer addressing the climate problem, which leaves too few speeches to measure their dispersion on these concepts.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-dispersion
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "Dispersion of positions by debate and party (standard deviation of speech-level positions; blank where fewer than 10 of the party's speeches address the concept)"
knitr::kable(tab_dispersion, format = "pipe", align = c("l", rep("r", 6)))
```

## Information Sources

Members frequently supported their claims with information from outside sources, as `r pct_any_src` percent of the speeches cited at least one. @tbl-sources shows the share of speeches in each debate that cite each type of source. In the cap-and-trade debate, science was the source cited most often by Democrats (`r ssal("science", "CT", "D")` percent of speeches), while Republicans most often cited the executive branch (`r ssal("executive", "CT", "R")` percent), science (`r ssal("science", "CT", "R")` percent), and unnamed experts (`r ssal("expert_generic", "CT", "R")` percent). Business sources were cited by about a fifth of Republican speeches in every debate, and by `r ssal("business", "CT", "D")`, `r ssal("business", "IRA", "D")`, and `r ssal("business", "OBBB", "D")` percent of Democratic speeches in the cap-and-trade, IRA, and OBBB debates, respectively.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-sources
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "Information sources by debate and party (percent of speeches citing at least one source of each type)"
knitr::kable(tab_sources, format = "pipe", align = c("l", rep("r", 6)))
```

Citations of science declined after the cap-and-trade debate. In the IRA debate, `r ssal("science", "IRA", "D")` percent of Democratic and `r ssal("science", "IRA", "R")` percent of Republican speeches cited science, and in the OBBB debate science was cited in `r ssal("science", "OBBB", "D")` percent of Democratic speeches and `r ssal("science", "OBBB", "R")` percent of Republican speeches. The scientific claims that members cited also differed by party. In the cap-and-trade debate, `r scons("CT", "R", "mainstream")` percent of Republican speeches cited science for a claim in line with the scientific consensus and `r scons("CT", "R", "dissenting")` percent cited science for a claim that disputes it. Among Democrats, `r scons("CT", "D", "mainstream")` percent cited science for a mainstream claim and `r scons("CT", "D", "dissenting")` percent for a dissenting claim. Dissenting science almost disappeared from the later debates.

Members rarely disputed the sources they cited, as only `r pct_dispute` percent of sources were disputed. The disputes that did occur were concentrated in sources associated with the other side. Republicans disputed `r sdis("science", "CT", "R")` percent of the science sources they cited in the cap-and-trade debate and `r sdis("executive", "IRA", "R")` percent of the executive branch sources they cited in the IRA debate, and Democrats disputed `r sdis("executive", "OBBB", "D")` percent of the executive branch sources they cited in the OBBB debate.

## Comparing the Debates

@tbl-salience shows the salience of each concept, or the share of speeches in each debate that address it. The cap-and-trade debate was organized around the instrument itself and its costs. Among Republicans, `r sal("PC4", "CT", "R")` percent of speeches addressed the costs of climate policy (PC4) and `r sal("SC1", "CT", "R")` percent addressed cap-and-trade (SC1). Democrats most often addressed the economic opportunity of clean energy (PC5, `r sal("PC5", "CT", "D")` percent), the risks of climate change (PC2, `r sal("PC2", "CT", "D")` percent), and energy security (PC7, `r sal("PC7", "CT", "D")` percent).

```{r}
#| label: tbl-salience
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "Salience of belief concepts by debate and party (percent of speeches that address the concept)"
knitr::kable(tab_salience, format = "pipe", align = c("l", rep("r", 6)))
```

The beliefs that were salient shifted in the later debates. Democrats continued to address the climate problem, and `r sal("PC2", "IRA", "D")` percent of Democratic speeches in the IRA debate addressed the risks of climate change. Yet Republicans largely stopped addressing it. The share of speeches that addressed PC1, PC2, or PC3 fell among Republicans from `r sci_talk["Cap-and-trade", "R"]` percent in the cap-and-trade debate to `r sci_talk["IRA", "R"]` percent in the IRA debate and `r sci_talk["OBBB", "R"]` percent in the OBBB debate, while among Democrats it was `r sci_talk["Cap-and-trade", "D"]`, `r sci_talk["IRA", "D"]`, and `r sci_talk["OBBB", "D"]` percent, respectively. In place of the climate problem, Republicans addressed fiscal restraint (DC4, `r sal("DC4", "IRA", "R")` percent in the IRA debate) and fossil fuel production (SC7, `r sal("SC7", "IRA", "R")` percent in the IRA debate and `r sal("SC7", "OBBB", "R")` percent in the OBBB debate). As a result, deep core beliefs made up a larger share of the statements in the IRA debate (`r tier_share["DC", "IRA D"]` percent of Democratic and `r tier_share["DC", "IRA R"]` percent of Republican statements) than in the cap-and-trade debate (`r tier_share["DC", "Cap-and-trade D"]` and `r tier_share["DC", "Cap-and-trade R"]` percent). The secondary beliefs also shifted from cap-and-trade to clean energy tax credits (SC5), which were addressed by `r sal("SC5", "OBBB", "D")` percent of Democratic and `r sal("SC5", "OBBB", "R")` percent of Republican speeches in the OBBB debate.

The two parties also emphasized different beliefs within each debate. The correlation between the salience of the concepts among Democrats and among Republicans was `r party_cor[["CT"]]` in the cap-and-trade debate, `r party_cor[["IRA"]]` in the IRA debate, and `r party_cor[["OBBB"]]` in the OBBB debate. In the OBBB debate, for instance, Democrats most often addressed costs (PC4, `r sal("PC4", "OBBB", "D")` percent) and economic opportunity (PC5, `r sal("PC5", "OBBB", "D")` percent), while Republicans most often addressed fossil fuel production (SC7, `r sal("SC7", "OBBB", "R")` percent). Thus, the parties disagreed not only in their positions but also in which beliefs they treated as relevant to the debate.

## Speeches About Climate and Energy

Some speeches addressed climate or energy only briefly. Climate or energy was the main subject of `r pct_focus[["CT"]]` percent of the speeches in the cap-and-trade debate, `r pct_focus[["IRA"]]` percent in the IRA debate, and `r pct_focus[["OBBB"]]` percent in the OBBB debate. However, limiting the analysis to these speeches does not change the results. Across concepts, debates, and parties, the correlation between the salience of each concept in the full sample and in the limited sample is `r cor_focus_sal`, and the correlation for mean positions is `r cor_focus_pos`. The correlation for the salience of the information sources is `r cor_focus_src`.

In the next section, I discuss what these results suggest about the feasibility of measuring belief systems with congressional speeches.
